archetype.name: Playoff Team (possession-first, goalie-questioned)
archetype.definition: Vegas drives play and generates shots like a top-10 team, and through 13 games it has had to overcome below-average goaltending and a leaky penalty kill to bank points.

report.headline: The skaters are winning the ice; the crease and the PK are giving it back.
report.take:
Vegas at 8-4-1 is second in the Pacific and 11th on the site, and the underlying game is better than that ranking suggests. Its 5-on-5 expected-goals share of .546 ranks 7th and its shot-attempt share of .53 ranks 9th. It puts 29.8 shots on goal a game, 7th in the league, while allowing 25, 11th. That is a team controlling territory, not one riding bounces. Its 5-on-5 PDO sits at 100.4, and Pts vs Goal Diff at -0.2 says the standings reflect the goal margin almost exactly. The record is real.

The engine is the forward group, graded A. Jack Eichel has 19 points with a .615 xGF share, and Mark Stone has 8 goals and 15 points at .609. The depth is what lifts the group above a one-line team. Tomas Hertl, Trevor Connelly and Ivan Barbashev all sit above .61 in xGF share, and Connelly's .656 leads the regulars. The blueline (B) has a clear top pair in results: Brayden McNabb is +13 and Shea Theodore +11. Rasmus Andersson is the soft spot at -7 with a sub-.500 xGF share.

The problems sit at both ends of the shot. The goalies are at -3.4 GSAx, 23rd, with a combined .886 save percentage. Carter Hart (-1.2) and Adin Hill (-2.0) are both below expected, so this is not one bad netminder dragging down a good one. It also isn't new: last season's team finished at -16.5 GSAx despite a .544 xGF share. The penalty kill at 67.7% ranks 28th, more than ten points under the league's 78.3%, and that is the cleanest explanation for the recent turn. A four-game winning streak gave way to three straight losses, including 2-6 defeats to Tampa Bay and St. Louis. Over the last five games Vegas is allowing 3.6 a game, well above its season rate.

The read is that Vegas is a legitimate playoff team whose ceiling depends on special teams and the crease. The power play (24.4%, 9th) and the 5-on-5 play are the kind of strengths that hold up. Neither the penalty kill nor the goaltending has a long track record of being this bad, and last year's 81.4% kill says the PK should climb back toward average. The goaltending is the bigger worry, because it was a problem a year ago too.

strengths.title: Five-on-five territorial control
strengths.body: Vegas wins the expected-goals and shot-attempt battles by clear margins and backs it with volume, ranking among the league's best in shots for while staying above average in shots against. Its 5-on-5 PDO is near neutral, so none of this leans on hot shooting. Possession driven by depth tends to hold up, and last season's .544 xGF share shows this is a repeatable profile.

strengths.title: Eichel and Stone lead an A forward group
strengths.body: Eichel and Stone rank 4th and 2nd on their position tabs. They are scoring at elite rates with xGF shares above .600, so the production is backed by chance share rather than percentages alone. Behind them, Hertl, Connelly and Barbashev all post plus chance shares, which is why the group grades A rather than leaning on one line.

strengths.title: A power play that converts
strengths.body: At 24.4% the power play ranks 9th and runs well above the league's 21.2%. Eichel, Stone and Marner each have five or six power-play points. Two seasons ago this unit ran at 28.3%, so an above-average power play fits this core.

concerns.title: Goaltending below expected, again
concerns.body: Both goalies are under water on GSAx, and the team's -3.4 ranks 23rd with a combined save percentage below the league's. It mirrors last season's -16.5, when strong chance share didn't translate because the crease leaked. Until Hart or Hill strings together league-average work, Vegas will lose games it outplays.

concerns.title: Penalty kill near the bottom
concerns.body: A 67.7% kill ranks 28th, far under the league average. It compounds the goaltending problem, since the kill depends on saves too. Last season's 81.4% suggests it should improve, but at this rate every penalty is close to a coin flip.

concerns.title: Goals against climbing lately
concerns.body: The last five games went 2-2-1, allowing 3.6 goals a game and turning the goal differential slightly negative. That closed with three straight losses, two of them by four goals. It is a small sample, but it lines up with the goaltending and PK weaknesses rather than any collapse in shot share.

trend.note: A 1-0 September and a four-game October winning streak built an 8-1-1 start, then a three-game skid with lopsided losses cooled things. The last ten are almost exactly at season rates, so the dip is recent rather than a sustained slide.

weekAhead.headline: Two winnable home games, then Boston and Pittsburgh on consecutive nights
weekAhead.body:
The week opens at home against Ottawa and New Jersey before a road back-to-back at Boston and Pittsburgh. Ottawa's 8-4-0 is padded by a 103 PDO and a +1.3 Pts vs Goal Diff, and it is being out-attempted at 5-on-5. Its power play ranks 29th, a rare chance for the Vegas kill to steady itself. New Jersey is the analytics heavyweight, first in both xGF % and CF %. Its D- goaltending makes it the one opponent whose crease is as shaky as Vegas's, so that game could turn into a track meet.

Boston is first on the site with a 107.6 PDO and +10.9 GSAx, the hottest finishing-and-goaltending team in the league. Its defense has held forwards to the second-fewest points against expectation. Vegas's shot volume should still tilt the ice, since Boston allows 27.8 shots a game, but beating that save percentage is the challenge. Pittsburgh on the second night is the softest matchup: it ranks 26th in holding forwards and 29th against wingers, and Vegas beat it 6-2 earlier this month. Two wins at home would make a split on the road acceptable.

keyMatchups.title: Vegas kill vs Ottawa's weak power play
keyMatchups.body: Ottawa converts just 11.5% of its power plays, 29th, which gives the 28th-ranked Vegas kill its best chance all week to post clean games. If the PK still leaks against this unit, the problem is structural rather than bad luck.

keyMatchups.title: Possession duel with New Jersey
keyMatchups.body: New Jersey leads the league in xGF % at .615, so for once Vegas may not win the territorial battle. Both teams have negative GSAx, which makes this a game the goalies could decide on their mistakes.

keyMatchups.title: Vegas forwards vs Pittsburgh's leaky defense
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh allows forwards well above their expected points and ranks 29th against wingers. That sets up Stone, Marner and Connelly on the back half of the back-to-back. Vegas's depth on the wings should matter most here.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Hart or Hill can post league-average save work against Boston, whose 107.6 PDO will punish any soft goal.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation holds up. A top-10 xGF share, strong shot volume, an A forward group and a productive power play look like the profile of a team that finishes comfortably in a playoff spot. The current pace of 107 points is reachable only if the penalty kill recovers toward average. It probably will, given that it was 81.4% last season. Even so, a more realistic landing spot is the high 90s to low 100s, because the goaltending has now been below expected for most of two seasons.

There is little regression risk in the record itself: PDO and Pts vs Goal Diff are both near neutral, so Vegas isn't living on luck. The upside is real if either goalie reaches average, because the skaters are already doing enough to make this a top-five team. The downside is a repeat of last year, when a strong-possession team finished with 95 points because the saves never came.
swingFactors: Hart and Hill reaching league-average save work
Penalty kill recovering toward the league's rate
Eichel and Stone sustaining elite chance share

confidence.note: Thirteen games is a small sample, but the shot and chance shares match last season's profile.
